# Eurostat Metabase Structure Monitor

Technical documentation. Covers what the system does, why it is built the way
it is, the data model, the processing pipeline, the subscription mechanism,
operational details, and known limitations.

---

## 1. Purpose and problem

Eurostat datasets change structure without notice: dimensions are renamed or
added, code lists gain or lose members, whole datasets are renamed or
withdrawn. These changes ship silently with Eurostat's twice-daily refresh
(11:00 and 23:00 CET). There is **no forward-looking schedule** of structural
changes anywhere in Eurostat's dissemination system, and the database keeps
only the latest version of each dataset — there is no versioning or history on
their side.

Downstream, this breaks things:

- Colleagues' Power Query links that hard-code dimension names and level
  codes in the API URL fail the moment a dimension is renamed or added.
- Automated R ingestion pipelines that assume a fixed structure break or, worse,
  silently mis-ingest.

The monitor's job is to **detect structural changes as soon as they publish**,
record them as durable history (which Eurostat itself does not keep), and
**alert the specific people who depend on the affected datasets** — before they
discover the breakage the hard way.

The system does not prevent breakage (it cannot; a renamed dimension breaks any
query that references it). It makes breakage **visible early and legible**, and
routes each change to the people who care about it.

---

## 2. Data source

The single source is the Eurostat **metabase** file:

```
https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/catalogue/metabase.txt.gz
```

It is a gzipped, tab-separated file giving the full structure of every
disseminated dataset, one row per `(dataset, dimension, position)`:

```
aact_ali01   geo    EU
aact_ali01   geo    EU27_2020
aact_ali01   itm_newa   40000
aact_ali01   time   2022
...
```

At the time of writing it is ~1.34M rows across ~7,600 datasets. Rows are
ordered by dataset, then dimension, then the code list's protocol order — this
row order is itself information (it is the intended order of the code list) and
is captured on ingest.

### Source constraints that shaped the design

- **No `Last-Modified` header.** The endpoint returns a chunked, generated
  response, so there is no file modification timestamp to use for change
  detection or as a publication time. This is confirmed behaviour, not a bug in
  the fetch. Consequently the observation timestamp we record is *our* fetch
  time, not Eurostat's publication time.
- **`NA` collides with Namibia.** Namibia's ISO-2 code is the literal string
  `NA`, which `data.table::fread` converts to a missing value by default. This
  must be suppressed on read (`na.strings = NULL`), or Namibia silently vanishes
  from every dataset that has it as a position, corrupting the structure record.
- **The metabase carries codes, not labels.** It gives dimension *codes* and
  position *codes*, never their human-readable titles. This is why some kinds of
  rename cannot be detected (see Limitations).

---

## 3. Architecture overview

The system separates into **reusable database components** (which belong in the
R package suite) and an **application** (the orchestration and alerting, which
is a standalone scheduled script). This separation is deliberate: the DB-generic
pieces are reused and warrant roxygen documentation and tests; the orchestration
is one specific job and is allowed to be a script.

| Concern | Belongs in | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Metabase SCD2 upsert (write) | UMARimportR | reusable, tested |
| Change-detection query (read) | UMARaccessR | reusable, tested |
| Subscription load/validate (write) | UMARimportR | reusable, tested |
| Orchestration, filtering, email | standalone script | application glue |

The application script wires these together and is what Windows Task Scheduler
runs. It is not a package because Task Scheduler runs a script, and because its
email/orchestration logic should not couple the general-purpose DB libraries to
this one monitoring use case.

All database objects live in a dedicated `eurostat` schema, separate from the
`platform` schema that holds the main statistical data model.

---

## 4. Data model

Three tables plus a temporary staging table, in the `eurostat` schema.

### 4.1 `snapshot` — one row per accepted ingest

```sql
CREATE TABLE eurostat.snapshot (
  snapshot_id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  file_sha256 text NOT NULL,          -- content identity of the ingested file
  observed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  n_rows      bigint NOT NULL
);
```

- `file_sha256` is the **content identity** of the metabase file. It is the
  dedup key: if the newly fetched file's hash matches the latest snapshot, there
  is nothing to do.
- `file_sha256` is **not** unique. A rollback (Eurostat reverting to a
  byte-identical earlier structure) is a real event we want to record as a new
  observation, so the same hash may legitimately appear on multiple dates.
  Uniqueness is on `snapshot_id` (the observation), not on content.
- `observed_at` is fetch time, not publication time (no header available).

### 4.2 `metabase` — the structural history (SCD2)

```sql
CREATE TABLE eurostat.metabase (
  dataset text NOT NULL,
  dim     text NOT NULL,
  pos     text NOT NULL,
  ord     int  NOT NULL,              -- protocol order within (dataset, dim)
  valid_from timestamptz NOT NULL,
  valid_to   timestamptz,             -- NULL = live
  from_snapshot_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES eurostat.snapshot(snapshot_id),
  to_snapshot_id   bigint          REFERENCES eurostat.snapshot(snapshot_id)
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_mb_live ON eurostat.metabase (dataset, dim, pos)
  WHERE valid_to IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX ix_mb_from ON eurostat.metabase (from_snapshot_id);
CREATE INDEX ix_mb_to   ON eurostat.metabase (to_snapshot_id);
```

This is a **Type-2 slowly-changing-dimension** table (SCD2). Each row represents one
`(dataset, dim, pos)` combination and the span over which it was live. A live
row has `valid_to IS NULL` / `to_snapshot_id IS NULL`. When a combination
disappears from the file, its row is *expired* (both `valid_to` and
`to_snapshot_id` set); when a new combination appears, a new live row is
inserted. Persisting combinations are left untouched.

Design decisions worth recording:

- **Only changed rows are written.** Each ingest expires the rows that vanished
  and inserts the rows that appeared; the vast unchanged majority are never
  rewritten. This keeps table churn tiny (dozens of rows on a normal day) and
  avoids the MVCC-bloat that an "expire everything, reinsert everything"
  approach would cause twice daily.
- **The unique partial index `ux_mb_live` enforces the core invariant:** at most
  one live row per `(dataset, dim, pos)`. A duplicate means an ingest bug, and
  the constraint turns that from silent corruption into an immediate,
  transaction-rolling-back failure.
- **`from_snapshot_id` / `to_snapshot_id` are the authoritative lineage keys.**
  They exist so that "which ingest created/expired this row" is answered by a
  foreign key, not by matching a timestamp. This is not cosmetic — see 4.4.
- **`ord` captures the code list's protocol order** at the time a row was
  inserted. It is used to build an ordered position signature for rename
  detection. It is **run-local**: it is not renumbered when a code is inserted
  mid-list in a later run, so ordinals can develop duplicates within a
  long-lived dimension. This is acceptable because it only ever makes rename
  detection *conservative* (a false negative, never a false positive), and no
  consumer relies on cross-run ordinal continuity. Reorder-without-rename is out
  of scope.
- **The `time` dimension is stored but never alerted on.** Every dataset's
  `time` dimension gains a position every period (new month/quarter/year), so it
  would be the single largest source of false alerts. It is kept in the store
  (it is real structure) and filtered out at detection time.

### 4.3 `subscription` — who wants to hear about what

```sql
CREATE TABLE eurostat.subscription (
  email   text NOT NULL,
  dataset text NOT NULL,              -- lowercased code, or '*' for all
  scope   text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'breaking' CHECK (scope IN ('breaking','all')),
  PRIMARY KEY (email, dataset)
);
```

- `email` is the natural key and the delivery address; there is no separate
  person column.
- `dataset = '*'` subscribes to all datasets.
- `scope` filters by change type: `breaking` (default) sends only changes that
  can break an existing query; `all` sends everything on the subscribed
  datasets. See 6.2 for the definition of "breaking".
- The `CHECK` constraint rejects any scope value other than the two allowed, so
  a typo in the source spreadsheet fails at load rather than silently producing
  a garbage filter.

### 4.4 Why lineage is keyed on snapshot id, not timestamp

An early version of the change-detection query joined rows to their snapshot by
matching `valid_from = snapshot.observed_at`. This is fragile: `timestamptz`
stores microsecond precision, and two values that *display* identically (both
shown to the millisecond) can differ in lower digits, so the equality silently
matches nothing. This produced a real bug where a query returned zero rows
despite visible changes in the table.

The fix, and the standing rule: **all change-detection keys off
`from_snapshot_id` / `to_snapshot_id` (integers), never off the timestamps.**
Integer equality has no precision to mismatch. The timestamp columns remain as
human-readable convenience only; the snapshot ids are authoritative.

---

## 5. Ingest pipeline

The ingest is a single function that takes an open connection and returns a
status description. It does not know that email or alerting exist — that is the
orchestrator's concern. It returns one of: `unchanged`, `changed` (with the new
`snapshot_id`), or raises an error.

Steps:

1. **Fetch** the gzipped metabase to a temp file and compute its `sha256`.
2. **Read** with `na.strings = NULL` (Namibia) and capture protocol order
   (`ord`) per `(dataset, dim)`.
3. **Dedup guard.** Compare the fetched `sha256` to the *latest* snapshot only.
   - Matches latest → `unchanged`, exit. Nothing to do.
   - Matches an *older* snapshot → a rollback. Warn, but proceed to ingest it as
     a new observation.
   - No match → a new structure, proceed.
4. **Diff and apply, in one transaction:**
   - Insert the new `snapshot` row first, capturing its id (needed as the FK for
     the rows about to change).
   - Load the fetched file into an unlogged temp staging table; `ANALYZE` it and
     index it so the planner uses hash joins, not nested loops.
   - **Bootstrap branch** (`n_live == 0`): the live set is empty, so every row
     is new by definition — a plain bulk insert, no anti-join. This exists
     because an anti-join against an empty target degenerates to a per-row scan
     and takes minutes; the plain insert takes seconds.
   - **Steady-state branch:** expire live rows absent from the file (anti-join
     staging → metabase), then insert file rows absent from the live set
     (anti-join metabase → staging). Both are sub-second at this scale with the
     FK indexes present.
5. **Return** `changed` with the new `snapshot_id`, `n_rows`, and a
   `rolled_back` flag.

The whole thing is wrapped so that on any exit — success, error, or early
return — the connection is disconnected. A **session-level advisory lock** taken
at the start makes the run a singleton: a second concurrent run exits
immediately rather than interleaving with the first. The lock releases
automatically on disconnect (session-scoped locks do not survive the session),
so no explicit unlock is needed.

---

## 6. Change detection

`compute_alerts(con, snapshot_id)` reads the metabase history and returns one
row per affected dataset for the given snapshot. It classifies at the dataset
level first, then breaks down dimension and level changes for datasets that were
neither newly added nor wholly removed.

### 6.1 Event types

| `event` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dataset_added` | Dataset appeared for the first time (no prior rows at all) |
| `dataset_removed` | Dataset had live rows before, none survive after |
| `changed` | Existing dataset with dimension and/or level changes |

For `changed` rows the query also returns:

- `dim_changes` — a text list like `geo:dim_added, unit:dim_removed`, or NULL if
  no dimension-level change.
- `level_added` / `level_removed` — counts of code-list positions added/removed
  (excluding `time`).

New and removed datasets are reported as a **single** event each; their
per-dimension changes are suppressed, because a whole-dataset event should not
also emit a `dim_added`/`dim_removed` for every one of its dimensions.

### 6.2 What counts as "breaking"

This is a **subscription** concept, not a detection concept, so it is defined in
the application (R), next to the subscription logic, not in the SQL. A change is
breaking if it can break an existing query:

- `dataset_removed`
- any dimension change (`dim_added` or `dim_removed`)
- `level_removed > 0`

Not breaking:

- `level_added` only — a new code rarely breaks anything that already runs
- `dataset_added` — a new dataset cannot break an existing query

`dim_added` is treated as breaking because an added dimension changes
granularity, which silently breaks downstream aggregations and joins — this is
precisely the failure that originally motivated the project.

---

## 7. Subscription system

### 7.1 The spreadsheet

Subscriptions are maintained by users themselves in a shared Excel file on the
network share. 

The location is: `"O:\Avtomatizacija\umar-automation-scripts\data\umar_data_bot_subscriptions\`
`eurostat_email_prijave.xlsx"`

Columns: `email`, `dataset`, `scope`, and an optional free-text
`notes` column that the system ignores entirely. One row per
`(email, dataset)`. Users add the dataset codes they depend on; `scope` defaults
to `breaking` if left blank; `dataset = *` opts into everything.

Putting the sheet where the knowledge lives (with the people who know their own
dependencies) is deliberate — it removes the maintainer as a bottleneck. The
spreadsheet is the human interface; the `subscription` table is the validated,
normalised truth derived from it.

### 7.2 Load and validation

`load_subscriptions(con)` reads the sheet and reloads the table. It:

1. **Selects columns by name**, so an extra column (like `notes`) cannot shift
   anything; a missing required column is a hard error.
2. **Normalises**: lowercases and trims email and dataset; defaults blank scope
   to `breaking`.
3. **Validates**, collecting problems without halting:
   - unknown dataset codes (checked against `SELECT DISTINCT dataset FROM
     metabase`, excluding `*`) — this is the critical check; a typo'd code that
     matches nothing would otherwise silently deliver no alerts,
   - invalid scope values,
   - duplicate `(email, dataset)` pairs.
   Bad rows are **skipped, not fatal** — one person's mistake must not block
   everyone else's subscriptions. Problems are emailed to the maintainer.
4. **Safety gate against corruption:** if the load would *remove* existing
   subscriptions for **more than one email address**, it refuses (raises) rather
   than applying the change. The editing convention is that no one touches
   another person's rows, so removals spanning multiple people mean the sheet
   was mangled (cleared, truncated, saved empty). A single person editing their
   own rows passes fine. This protects the authoritative table from a corrupted
   sheet without a merge engine — it is a sanity gate, not a diff.
5. **Truncate + reload** the clean rows, in one transaction. The sheet is
   authoritative, so idempotent full replacement is the simplest correct model;
   the gate handles the "authoritative until someone breaks it" case.

`load_subscriptions` runs on **every** run, not only on change days, so that a
corrupted sheet surfaces (via the gate) the same night it happens rather than
lying in wait until the next structural change.

---

## 8. Alerting

The orchestrator (`main`) runs, in order:

1. Connect, take the advisory lock, configure email auth.
2. `load_subscriptions` — validate the human input first, fail fast if corrupt.
3. `ingest` — wrapped so any failure emails the maintainer and still records the
   traceback in the log.
4. If `unchanged`, exit.
5. If `changed`: `compute_alerts` → filter per subscriber → send one email per
   affected subscriber. This whole stage is wrapped so a failure in the alert
   query or send emails the maintainer rather than dying silently in the log.

### 8.1 Per-person filtering

`filter_alerts` joins the run's alert rows to the subscription table:

- `dataset = '*'` matches all alert rows; otherwise exact dataset match.
- `scope = 'breaking'` keeps only breaking rows (6.2); `scope = 'all'` keeps
  everything for the matched datasets.

One email is sent per affected subscriber, containing only their matched rows,
and only if they have at least one, silence on non-events.

### 8.2 Email format

Alerts are HTML email with the change table wrapped in `<pre>` for a monospace
font, so the space-padded columns actually align.

A `dataset_removed` row carries an added note suggesting the dataset may have
been renamed and to check for a replacement code. This is a cheap mitigation of
the rename-detection gap (Section 10): the system cannot yet link a removal to
its replacement, but it can tell the affected subscriber to go look.

### 8.3 Two distinct email concerns

- **Operational failure** (ingest broke, sheet corrupt, alert query failed) →
  goes to the maintainer. Distinctive subject prefix for inbox filtering.
- **Structural alert** (something changed) → goes to subscribers.

These are separate functions with separate recipients and must not be merged.

---

## 9. Operations

- **Schedule:** Windows Task Scheduler runs a batch script a few minutes after
  the Eurostat evening refresh (~23:00 CET), and after the 11:00
  refresh. The task name is `eurostat-update-metabase`. Exact timing is not critical: the `sha256` dedup makes a catch-up run
  after downtime free (it exits immediately if nothing changed).
- **Batch wrapper:** the batch script calls `Rscript` with
  `source(...); tryCatch(main(), error = ...)` so that an R-level failure sets a
  non-zero exit code (Task Scheduler otherwise reports success on any R error),
  and `pushd` into the repo before the git steps so committing the log works.
- **Logging:** stdout/stderr are redirected to a `.Rout` file on the share,
  which is committed to git for an audit trail. The `.Rout` is overwritten each
  run; git preserves the history. The log is *not* the alert channel — alerts
  and failures are emailed from within the script via `gmailr`.
- **Alert channel is email only.** Failure surfaces as a maintainer email plus a
  log entry; there is no second channel.
- **Secrets:** the DB password is read from an environment variable; the Gmail
  OAuth credentials and token cache are at absolute paths on the share. The
  scheduled account must be able to read the credentials and write the token
  cache.

---

## 10. Known limitations and backlog

Recorded honestly so a future maintainer knows the edges.

- **Dataset renames are not linked.** A renamed dataset appears as an unrelated
  `dataset_removed` (old code) and `dataset_added` (new code). The system
  detects both but cannot connect them, because the metabase carries codes, not
  titles. The `dataset_removed` alert includes a "check for a replacement" hint
  as a stopgap. *Fix (backlog):* snapshot the Table of Contents (`toc.txt`/`xml`),
  which carries dataset code **and** title, and match a removed title to an added
  title to identify renames near-decisively. This is the one substantive
  detection gap and is the direct analogue of the failure that motivated the
  project, one level up (table renamed rather than dimension renamed).

- **Level (code) renames are not distinguished from drop+add.** A code renamed
  within a dimension shows as `level_removed` + `level_added`, unlinked, for the
  same reason (no labels in the metabase).

- **Dimension renames rely on a heuristic.** A dimension rename shows as
  `dim_removed` + `dim_added` in the same dataset and run; a matching ordered
  position signature makes it near-decisive, but it remains a candidate, not a
  certainty. (The signature logic was prototyped but is not currently wired into
  `compute_alerts`; fold it back in when a real dimension rename first occurs.)

- **Reorder-without-rename is not detected.** If Eurostat reorders a code list
  without changing membership, no rows change, so nothing fires; `ord` on
  surviving rows also goes stale. Out of scope by choice — reordering does not
  break code-based queries.

- **The observation timestamp is fetch time, not publication time**, because the
  endpoint provides no `Last-Modified`. Change *ordering* is preserved by
  snapshot id; only the absolute "when did Eurostat publish this" is
  approximate.

- **Automated pipeline dependencies are not auto-subscribed.** A dataset that
  the agency's own R ingestion depends on will only be alerted on if someone has
  manually added it to the subscription sheet. *Fix (backlog):* subscribe the
  ingestion pipelines' own dataset lists to a bot-monitored address, so a table
  a pipeline relies on cannot vanish unnoticed. (This is exactly the case that
  broke a package test when `agr_r_animal` was silently replaced.)

- **OAuth token expiry is the most likely silent-death mode.** If the Gmail
  refresh token expires or the token cache becomes unwritable by the scheduled
  account, all alerting fails silently — no alerts, no failure emails. *Mitigation:*
  periodically confirm alerts still arrive; consider a heartbeat or second
  channel if the system becomes critical.
  
- **Comtex data monitoring gap**  Comtex (detailed trade, `ds-*`) is a spearate dissemenation system not covered by the metabase monitor. Structural changes in those datasets are not detected. These are also currently not ingested by EUROSTATfetchR, so it's a moot point for now anyway. 

---

## 11. Design principles applied throughout

For future changes, the principles this system was built on:

- **Detect, don't schedule.** Eurostat publishes no change schedule; monitoring
  is necessarily proactive and after-the-fact-but-before-consumption.
- **Fail loud.** Every stage that can fail either raises or emails the
  maintainer; nothing swallows an error silently. The one thing a monitor must
  never do is fail quietly.
- **One source of truth per fact.** Redundant columns encoding the same thing
  (a flag plus a timestamp; a stored classification plus the data it derives
  from) were rejected in favour of deriving one from the other. Derived-and-cached
  is acceptable; stored-as-a-second-primary drifts.
- **Content identity over metadata.** Dedup on the file's hash, not on unreliable
  timestamps or headers.
- **Keys over coincidences.** Lineage joins on integer snapshot ids, never on
  timestamp equality.
- **Complexity must be justified by scale.** At ~1.3M rows, several performance
  defences (fingerprint tiers, full-snapshot storage avoidance) were considered
  and dropped as unnecessary. The design is sized to the actual data, not an
  imagined order of magnitude larger.
- **Reusable components are packages with tests; applications are scripts.** The
  DB-generic pieces belong in UMARimportR/UMARaccessR with roxygen and dittodb
  fixtures; the orchestration is glue and stays a standalone script.
